Business Owners: STAY AWAY from Hibu Marketing. Consider this your warning.

**Business Owners: STAY AWAY from Hibu Marketing. Consider this your warning.**  
I cannot believe how absolutely awful my experience with Hibu has been. If you’re a small business owner considering them, PLEASE do your homework before signing anything.  
The salesperson told me everything I wanted to hear to get my signature. I specifically requested $3,000/month toward Google Ads. I was told 100% would go toward advertising because Hibu “makes their money elsewhere.” Turns out only about $1,500 was actually allocated to Google Ads, with the rest going toward other services.  
I was also told I could change my Google Ads budget at any time. That turned out to be another promise that wasn’t honored.  
And their supposedly “custom” websites? I discovered another auto repair shop IN MY SAME CITY, with the SAME SALESPERSON, had essentially the same website, right down to the stock photo!  
I’ve had TWO website services canceled and an SEO package terminated after numerous issues.  
The incompetence and lack of communication have been unbelievable. In my experience, if you actually care about your business, plan on babysitting everything, catching mistakes yourself, and doing the work you’re supposedly paying these people to handle.  
Here’s the part that absolutely blows my mind.  
**I FIRED THEM. I hired another company. I told Hibu to stop advertising my business. I even sent a cease-and-desist.**  
Their response? They refuse to terminate my Google Ads contract. Instead, they’ve repeatedly offered me credits toward services I have made abundantly clear I DO NOT WANT.  
**It’s MY business. MY reputation. And I no longer want this company representing either one.**  
I’ve never encountered a company so determined to hold on to an unhappy customer rather than simply part ways.  
I’m sharing my experience because I wish someone had warned me before I signed. Get EVERY sales promise in writing, demand a breakdown of where every advertising dollar goes, and read the cancellation terms carefully.  
**My experience with Hibu has been an absolute nightmare. Other small business owners deserve to know what they’re potentially signing up for.**

Everything in B2B outbound is automated now, and buyers are exhausted

Buyers are not tired of receiving messages. They are tired of receiving messages that require them to do the sender’s thinking.

You know the type.

“We help companies like yours achieve X.”

“Would improving Y be a priority?”

“Just bumping this to the top of your inbox.”

The message gives the buyer no proof that the sender understands their situation. It asks them to stop, interpret a generic promise, decide whether it might apply, and then spend time explaining their problem back to a stranger.

Automation made sending cheap. It did not make attention cheap.

I think the next advantage in outbound will come from sending fewer messages with better reasons, not from generating more human sounding variations.

A useful message should do some of the work before it arrives. It should show why this person was selected, what situation the sender noticed, and what hypothesis they have about the problem. The buyer should only need to say, “yes, relevant,” “not now,” or “you have this wrong.”

There is another part people miss. Once the buyer replies, the automation often becomes obvious. The system repeats a question they answered, sends a scheduled follow up, or hands them a generic response. That is where trust disappears.

Automate research, organization, reminders, and the boring parts. Keep judgment and live conversation close to a human.

Buyers are exhausted because the cost of sending dropped while the effort put into relevance also dropped.

What is the fastest way an automated message loses your attention?

where do you draw the line between quoting a job and designing it for free?

I’m involved in my family's marble business.

Most of our traditional work is straightforward enough to quote, slabs, dimensions, finish, quantity, transport, etc.

But we've started taking on more custom marble fabrication and finished-product enquiries, and I'm running into a problem I hadn't appreciated before.

Someone sends us a photograph of an object and says:

**“Can you make this in marble? What would it cost?”**

To the customer, that's a request for a price.

For us, answering it properly might mean figuring out:

Will the design even work in stone?

What thickness will stop it breaking?

Can the inside actually be machined?

Does it need two pieces rather than one?

How will hardware be fixed?

Will it stand safely?

How much hand finishing will it need?

How do we pack it?

And only after all of that can we estimate cost properly.

By that point, we've sometimes done a meaningful amount of product development for someone who may have casually sent the same image to ten manufacturers.

But I don't want to swing too far the other way either.

If somebody sends a simple enquiry and gets back a form asking 18 questions plus a design fee, we've created friction before they even know whether the project is remotely in budget.

For people doing custom fabrication/manufacturing — furniture, metalwork, millwork, stone, signage, etc. — how do you handle this?

I'm considering something like:

very rough feasibility + price range for free,

then paid prototyping/engineering once the customer wants an accurate quote, with the fee credited against a production order.

Does that work in practice?

Where do you personally draw the line between **sales effort** and **unpaid engineering**?

Would I be in the wrong to request a partial refund from my website designer?

I hired a website designer in January to do my branding and website for my business. I paid almost $3000 for the package, and the original timeline was around 8–12 weeks for both branding and the website.

To summarize: her contract says no refunds will be completed after the design process has started. We have a signed contract but it basically only protects her. I didn’t think this would be an issue because I have several friends in the industry who have used her for their websites and they turned out great. 

Since the beginning, there have been constant delays and communication issues. She'll tell me something will be ready “today” or “next week,” and then the deadline comes and goes, and I have to follow up multiple times to get an update. She commits to something and then comes up with an excuse, and I am always the one who has to check in. This has happened over and over again, and it's honestly exhausting.

I do want to acknowledge that I had a pretty serious concussion and skull fracture earlier this year, and I also dealt with psychosis when weaning off meds, which delayed me getting some photos uploaded until August, when I was supposed to have it done in June. I completely understand that this pushed things back on my end, and I'm not expecting her to have worked on my website while I was dealing with that. But the missed deadlines and lack of communication were happening well before that, and are happening again.

I uploaded my photos on August 1st and sent her an email to let her know everything was uploaded. On August 10th, I sent another email after no response. Later that day, she said that she had been traveling (no OOO message) and said she was catching up on her inbox. On August 26th, I emailed again, checking in. On August 28th, she said she was “still working away” and would be done the next week. On September 13th, I reached out again, asking how things were going with my website, and mentioned how she had said it would be done two weeks again. On September 15th she sent a typo-ridden email saying “it’s been crazy town over here” and said she would be done by Tuesday next week at the latest. September 21st I reach out to check in, and on September 25th she says she has a “nasty cold” and will need “a few extra days” to get everything uploaded.

I have been so patient and kind, have always taken her excuses at face value, and have never been anything but friendly to her. This pattern just keeps repeating and she has disappointed me so many times.

We’re now almost 9 months into this project without a finished website or even any branding materials, which I also paid for. Reminder, the contract says 8-12 weeks. I have had to chase this girl every step of the way to get anything done. I know I took a two month hiatus, but if she had been responsive in the first few months, we could’ve finished the project before my health issues even started.

I'm not necessarily looking to cancel the project, but I'm getting to the point where I feel like I should ask for a partial refund. I didn't pay almost $3,000 to have to constantly remind someone that I'm their client and follow up on things they promised.  
I know she's a small business owner, and I don't want to be unfair. But I'm just so frustrated and feel like she’s totally failed on her end.

AIO for wanting a partial refund, or am I being unreasonable?
